goal: A project that reads `ready` is one the runner would actually start. Where it would not, the same reading names what is in the way, since when, and which run left it — in `mc status <name>`, on the page and in the brief.

Measured 2026-09-05: memoro-cli's only two unfinished plans, `intake-inbox` and `role-instructions`, both read `ready` in every surface while `~/mc/runner/held.json` held #612 and #614 at `repairs: 0`. The whole repository's queue was stopped and no reading said so. The one place that knew was `runner.log`, which carried 9 827 `, skip` lines.
contract: Martin, 2026-09-05: *"Om något är 'ready' så ska det kunna köras av runner. Som det är nu är flera projekt 'ready' enligt status, men i praktiken 'blocked'."*

No new status value in the plan schema, and no machine state written into a repository. The plan is on `main` and the reasons are on this machine; a step session may not write plan state anyway. `planState` and `planSummary` (`src/mc/plan-schema.js:258`, `:273`) keep exactly the meaning they have — the state of the first step that is not done.

The new reading and `runStepClaimed` may not drift. Whatever the round refuses on is what the reading reports, and that is asserted by a test over a table of cases rather than by two lists maintained by hand.
The reading starts nothing, writes nothing and asks no model — the rule `status-collect.js` opens with, because `mc status` and the page are read while the runner is working.
out_of_scope: The 12 plans blocked on `plan-review`. Martin, 2026-09-05: *"Plan-review = djup genomgång per projekt för att se om det ska startas upp på nytt och isf i vilken form. Med största sannolikhet behöver projektet arbetas om. Jag sätter igång ett i taget."* They are a backlog worked one at a time, `blocked` is the honest status for each, and nothing here changes it.

Building the runner's own recovery of a killed session's uncommitted work. Step 4 measures the question and puts it; whether the runner commits such a worktree itself is a later project, if Martin wants one.
What the gate holds and how a repair session runs. `heldRepair` and the one-repair rule are read by this project and changed by it in no way.
The plan schema, `chooseKind`, and the order the runner walks projects in. This project adds a second reading beside the existing one; it moves no decision into it.
`runner.log`'s own lines. They stay exactly as they are — the defect is that nothing else says any of it, not that the log says it badly.

success_criteria.criterion: A project the runner cannot start does not read `ready` alone in any surface a person uses.
success_criteria.check: With #612 and #614 held as they are today, `mc status intake-inbox` and `mc status role-instructions` each name the held pull request beside the plan state, and the page's queue block does too. Run both commands and read them.

success_criteria.criterion: The reading and the round agree on every reason the round refuses.
success_criteria.check: A test drives a table of cases — STOP file, dirty worktree, GitHub unknown, held with a repair spent, open pull request, branch that will not check out, aborted merge — against both the new reading and the round's own path, and asserts the same answer from each. A reason added to `runStepClaimed` without the reading fails it.

success_criteria.criterion: A `ready` project skipped for a dirty worktree is named where a person looks, with the age of the dirt and the run that left it.
success_criteria.check: Make a workarea dirty by hand, run `mc brief --collect`, and read the section: the project, how long it has been dirty, and the `runs.tsv` row that left it. Remove the file afterwards and confirm the line goes.

success_criteria.criterion: The reading costs no git work on a project the plan already refuses.
success_criteria.check: The function short-circuits on `kindFor`'s answer before touching a worktree; asserted by a test whose git dependency throws if called.

steps.title: The machine-state reading, beside kindFor
steps.done_when: One function answers "would the runner start this project now, and if not what is in the way" from the files on this machine, and a test asserts it agrees with the round over a table of cases.
instruction: Half of this already exists and is already shared. `kindFor(name, { plans })` in `src/mc/status-collect.js:48` flattens `chooseKind` to one string — the kind, or `skip:<reason>` for a plan that is blocked, done, unparseable or unmigrated — and both the page (`page-collect.js:281`) and the runner (`run.js:1532`, as `planRefusal`) call it. That is the plan-shaped half and it is correct. Do not touch it.

The missing half is named by the code itself. `refusedLine`'s comment at `run.js:1544` says it outright: *"What it costs is the lines that are not on the page: a dirty worktree, a pull request in flight, a merge that conflicted. Those are facts about this machine at this moment, they keep their own named line in `runStep`."* Those lines are the whole defect. Write the sibling function beside `kindFor` in `status-collect.js`, because that is where the page's readers live and the module's own rule — no model, nothing written, nothing started — is the rule this needs.

The reasons, in the order `runStepClaimed` (`src/mc/run.js:1198`) asks them, because the reading has to answer with the first one the round would hit and not merely with some true one: the STOP file (`stopRequested()`, `paths.stop`); no workarea and no plan on main (`repoOf`); a dirty worktree (`git status --porcelain` in the workarea, `run.js:1222`); the repository GitHub could not be asked (`prsFailed`); a held pull request whose repair is spent (`heldRepair` over `heldNow()`, and note that a held entry at `repairs: 0` is *not* a refusal — it is one repair session owed, which is a thing the runner would start); an open pull request (`inFlight(openPrs)`); a branch the workarea could not check out (`freshBranch`, and the repair path's `git checkout` at `run.js:1250`); and a merge of `origin/main` that conflicted (`syncMain`, `run.js:414`).

Return enough for a person, not just a word. `{ runnable, reason, detail, since }` at least: `reason` a word the page can count, the way `kindFor`'s is; `detail` the sentence — the held pull request's number, the first three dirty files, the conflicted paths; `since` when it started being true, read from `held.json`'s `since` for a hold and from the mtime of the oldest dirty path for a worktree. `since` is what makes the difference between a project that stalled a minute ago and `connections-section`, which stood six days.

Order matters for cost as well as for truth. Ask `kindFor` first and return its answer without touching the workarea — a project whose plan on main already refuses it must cost no `git status`, no fetch and no merge. That is the same economy `planRefusal` was built for (`run.js:1509`: a round spent 51 seconds walking 38 projects to start one). Assert it with a test whose git dependency throws if it is called.

The agreement test is the point of the step, not an extra. Build the table of cases once and drive both the new function and the round's own path from it, so a reason added to `runStepClaimed` without the reading fails the suite. Two lists maintained by hand is the failure this is meant to prevent, and a test that only exercises the new function does not prevent it. `tests/mc/run.test.js` already fixtures the round with injected `deps` — reuse that shape rather than inventing a second one.

Do not read a lease. A repository lease held by a gate round or a deploy is a reason a round waits rather than a reason a project cannot run, and it is gone within minutes; putting it in this reading would make `mc status` flicker. If reading `repo-lease.js` convinces you otherwise, say so in the PR rather than adding it quietly.
`npm test`.
comments: The reading is `machineState(name, world)` in `src/mc/status-collect.js`, beside `kindFor`. It takes read data — `plans`, `prs`, `prsFailed`, the parsed `held.json`, whether the STOP file is there, the work root — plus three injected readers: `exists`, a `git` that is only ever given read-only arguments, and `mtime`. It returns `{ runnable, reason, detail, since, kind }`. `kind` is what the runner would start, `step` or `repair`, so step 2 can say `ready · repair owed` as easily as `ready · held #614`.

The anti-drift mechanism is a shared vocabulary, not a second list. `RUN_REFUSALS` in `run-plan.js` is every word a round refuses on for a reason that is not in the plan, in the order `runStepClaimed` asks them; `runStepClaimed` now returns `skipped:<reason>` through one `refuse()` helper, and the reading answers in the same words. Three tests hold it together in `tests/mc/run.test.js`: a table of twelve cases driven through both the round (`runner.runStep`) and the reading over one fixture, a coverage test asserting every word in `RUN_REFUSALS` has a case, and a source check that no refusal returns a bare `'skipped'` (the lane claim in `runStep` is the one exception, and it is a fact about this process rather than about the files).

Four of the eleven words carry `read: false` and a `why`: `worktree`, `sync`, `role-missing`, `tool-missing`. Each is the outcome of work the round did and the reading may not do — creating a worktree, fetching and merging, reading a role out of a synced worktree, spawning a tool. For those the table asserts the reading says *runnable* rather than guessing, which is the honest answer: `mc status` cannot know a fetch will fail. So `runnable: true` means nothing on this machine is standing in the way, not that the round is guaranteed to start.

`no-repo` is deliberately not a word. A name with neither a workarea nor a plan on main is `no-plan` — `kindFor`'s own word, which the reading reaches one question earlier than the round does. The round now says `no-plan` there too.

A merge left in a workarea is reported as `dirty`, because that is what the round does with it: an unmerged path makes `git status --porcelain` non-empty and the round skips on that, before any of its own merge work. The reading tells the two apart in `detail` — `a merge stopped in <worktree>: …` against `uncommitted work in <worktree>: …` — since a person needs to know which it is. There is no separate `merge` word, and adding one would make the two readings disagree.

Run against the estate on 2026-09-05 with a read-only script (`listPlans` over both repos, `gh pr list`, the real `held.json`, real git): 43 unfinished plans, and the two that read `ready` while nothing could start them are named — `connections-section` as `dirty since 2026-09-05T10:03:51Z — uncommitted work in /Users/martinforsberg/mc/connections-section/memoro: hop-measure.mjs, probe.mjs`, and this workarea itself. Nothing else disagreed with its plan state.

For step 2's check: `held.json` is now `[]` — #612 and #614 have both been repaired and landed, and `intake-inbox` and `role-instructions` are off main entirely. The estate example that survives is `connections-section`'s dirty worktree; a hold to look at will have to be made by hand, as that step's instruction allows.

steps.title: mc status and the page say the pair
steps.done_when: `mc status <name>` and the page show the plan state and the machine state together, and `ready` on its own means the runner would start it.
instruction: `mc status <name>` today prints `planSummary(plan).status` and nothing about this machine: `fieldRows` in `src/mc/status-project.js:41` builds the rows, and the file's own header says the plan is read from the workarea when there is one and from `origin/main` otherwise. It shows open pull requests on the branch (`openPrsFor`) but never `held.json` and never the worktree. That is why `mc status role-instructions` reads `ready` while #614 is held.

Put the pair in the status row rather than in a new row below it. `ready · held #614` is the shape the proposal asked for and it reads correctly aloud; a second row named something like `runnable` invites a reader to take the first row as the answer and stop. Where the machine has nothing to say, the row is exactly what it is today — that is the case that must not get noisier.

The page's queue block already counts plan-shaped skips: `queueSection` in `src/mc/page-collect.js:277` maps each queued name through `kindFor` and groups `skip:<reason>` into `skipped: { count, reasons }`. Extend that with the machine-state reasons from step 1 so the block's counts stop being a partial answer — a queue that reports two runnable names while both are held is worse than one that reports none.

Keep the page's discipline: `page-collect.js` and `status-collect.js` are pure and take read data. If the new reading needs `held.json` and the open pull requests, they are already read on the page's path (`heldEntries(readJson(heldPath(root)))` at `page-collect.js:746`) — pass them in, do not read the filesystem from a builder.

Verify against the estate as it actually stands: run `mc status intake-inbox`, `mc status role-instructions` and the page, and put what they print in the PR. If both holds have been repaired by the time you run it, make one by hand instead and say so.
`npm test` — `tests/mc/status-project.test.js` and the page tests read these.
comments: The pair rides on the status row of `mc status <name>`: `fieldRows(plan, problems, machine, home)` in `src/mc/status-project.js` builds `ready · <the machine's own sentence> (since MM-DD hh:mmZ)`. `machineNote` is the rule for when it says nothing, and there are three cases and no others: a refusal the plan already names is dropped (`blocked · blocked` is the row it exists to stop), `runnable` is silent, and the one loud `runnable` case is a hold still owed its repair — because what the runner would start there is a repair and not the step the plan names. The home directory is folded to `~` in the sentence, since a workarea's absolute path is most of a terminal row.

`collectProject` asks the reading of the plan on **origin/main**, not of the workarea copy the rows above it show, because origin/main is the copy the round reads. When the two differ the plan row already says `differs from origin/main`, and a plan that is `ready` in the workarea while main's is `blocked` now says so on the status row as well. The reading is given the project's siblings on main as bare `{ project, repo }` entries — without them a pull request on `mc-cut-2` reads as `mc`'s (project-prs.js).

`queueSection` (`src/mc/page-collect.js`) takes an injected `machine: (name) => …` rather than reading the filesystem itself, which is that module's rule; `collectPage` passes one built from `machineState` over the plans, the PR list, `held.json`, the STOP file and a read-only `git`. A caller that passes none gets exactly the plan-shaped block it got before, which is what the older page tests still assert. A skipped name's kind becomes `skip:<machine word>` so the existing count-by-reason picks it up for free, and a runnable name's kind is what the runner would actually start — `repair` where a hold is owed one, which needed a colour in `KIND_TONE` and therefore a row in the palette table of `docs/technical/mc-ui.md` (a test binds the two).

What GitHub was not asked is not the same as nothing being open, and both surfaces now say so rather than promising a `ready` they cannot stand behind: `mc status --offline` and a failed `gh` both leave the repository in `prsFailed`, and on the page so does a missing PR cache (`prs.fetched` null) or a `gh pr list` that failed under `--fresh`. The consequence to know about is that `mc status --offline <name>` reads `ready · GitHub could not be asked what this repository has open` for every project. It is the round's own word for it, and there is a test naming that choice.

Verified live on 2026-09-05 against the estate, in a shadow work root under `/tmp` with `MC_WORK_ROOT`, because `held.json` was `[]` and the runner (pid 9053) was running — writing a hand-made hold into `~/mc/runner/held.json` could have started a repair session on it. The shadow root held symlinks to four real workareas, a queue.md naming them, and a hold made by hand against this step's own pull request. Four readings: held with its repair spent (`ready · #631 is held before merge after a repair — the brief's (since 09-03 10:00Z)`, and `skipped 2 (held-after-repair 1, dirty 1)` on the page); the same hold at `repairs: 0` (`… one repair session is owed`, and `runner-visibility  repair` at the top of the queue); no hold at all (`#631 is open … — not starting a step`, `skipped 2 (in-flight 1, dirty 1)`); and `mc status total-lane-cap`, which has nothing in the way and printed the bare `ready` it printed before. The dirty case is real rather than made: `mc status connections-section` against the true `~/mc` reads `ready · uncommitted work in ~/mc/connections-section/memoro: hop-measure.mjs, probe.mjs (since 09-05 10:03Z)`. The shadow root was removed afterwards; nothing under `~/mc` was written.

For step 3: the brief is the surface this step did not touch, and `connections-section` is still dirty on this machine, so that step's own check can be run against it without making anything. The reading it needs is the same `machineState` call — `brief-collect.js` already reads `held.json` (`HELD_FILE`) and `runsFor`, and the four things a line needs (name, reason, since, the run that left it) are `reason`, `detail`, `since` and a `runs.tsv` row.

steps.title: The brief names what is waiting on hands
steps.done_when: `mc brief --collect` has a section listing every `ready` project the runner cannot start, one line each, with the reason and how long it has been true.
instruction: The brief is the surface that matters most here, because it is the one Martin reads at a decision point and the one a brief session acts on. It already has the shape: *Held before merge* is a short section, one line per project, built from `~/mc/runner/held.json` filtered to what the brief is for (`src/mc/brief-collect.js:360`, `HELD_FILE` at `:437`).

What it does not cover is everything else in step 1's reading, and the gap is not theoretical: `held.json` is *for a pull request the gate refused*, and a session killed before it committed never got as far as a pull request. `no-text-in-code` sat from 2026-09-04T12:37Z on exit 143 with 35 files of finished work uncommitted; `connections-section` sat from 2026-08-29T21:37Z on a session that exited 0 and opened no pull request. Neither is in `held.json`, neither is in *Workareas with no project on main* — both have a project on main, which is exactly why they are a loss — and both were skipped every round with one log line nothing reads.

One line per project, with the four things a person needs to act: the name, the reason, since when, and the run that left it. `no-text-in-code: uncommitted since 12:37, step exit 143` is the proposal's own example and it is the right density. The run comes from `runsFor` in `brief-collect.js`, which the brief already reads.

Decide from the code whether this is a new section or rows inside *Held before merge*, and say which and why in the PR. A held pull request and a dirty worktree are both "the runner is waiting on hands", which argues for one section; they need different actions from the reader, which argues for two. Either is defensible — an undefended choice is not.

The brief session has to be told what to do with it, or a new section is a new thing to skim past. Whatever `canon/roles/brief.md` says about *Held before merge* is the precedent to follow for the new rows.

Verify for real: make a workarea dirty by hand, run `mc brief --collect`, read the section, then clean it up and confirm the line goes. Note that a verification brief left in `~/mc/brief/` moves `lastBriefTime` — it is the mtime of the newest file there — so remove the file you wrote, as step 1 of `intake-inbox` had to.
`npm test`.
comments: A section of its own, *Ready, and the runner cannot start it*, between *Held before merge* and *Queue* — not rows inside *Held before merge*. The two are the same waiting and not the same act: every row of *Held before merge* is a pull request and takes one of that section's three answers (`canon/roles/brief.md` — merge by hand, close, block the step), and none of the three exists for a workarea a killed session left uncommitted, where the act is to open the worktree and decide what the work was. A row under prose that promises the wrong answer is a row somebody applies the wrong answer to. The held projects still appear in the new section, in the reason word and no further, so it is the whole answer to "what says ready and does not run" without a second copy of the gate's detail that could disagree with the first.

`waitingOnHands` is the builder (`brief-collect.js`), pure like the rest of the module: it takes the plans, an injected `machine` reader and the runs.tsv text, and keeps only the refusals whose word is in `RUN_REFUSALS`. That filter is what makes it *ready* projects — `blocked`, `done` and `unparseable` are `chooseKind`'s words, they are *Plan status*'s rows, and a reason added to the round arrives here without a second list to maintain. `collectBrief` builds the reader from `machineState` over the plans, the open pull requests, the whole `held.json` (not `heldForBrief`'s filtered half — an entry at `repairs: 0` is a repair the runner would start), the STOP file and a read-only `git`.

Two shapes of noise were designed out, and both are worth keeping. `prs-unknown` is a fact about a repository, not a project — true of every ready plan it has — so it is one line per repository rather than twenty rows burying the one that is somebody's; and a project the runner has a live session on is dropped entirely, because its worktree is dirty precisely because somebody is working in it. That second one was found by running the thing: at 2026-09-05T16:35Z the section named `sql-w3-email-closure`, eight minutes into its step. `readCurrents` moved to `status-collect.js` for it (page-collect.js imports brief-collect.js, so the traffic could only go the other way), and only a lane file whose pid is alive counts — a crashed runner's leftover file is exactly the workarea this section is for.

`machineDetail(machine, home)` also moved to `status-collect.js`, beside the reading it renders: `mc status <name>` had the home-folding sentence and the brief needed the same one, and status-project.js imports brief-collect.js so it could not be shared from there. `collectBrief` gained a `batch` dependency beside `git` — the round already passes `showBatch(gitOut)` (run.js), and without it no test can put a plan on `origin/main` without a real repository. The open-PR listing now asks for the round's own `PR_FIELDS` plus `createdAt`, so `describePr` draws a draft as a draft.

Verified live against the estate on 2026-09-05, running this worktree's `node src/mc-cli.js brief --collect`. With `connections-section` dirty as it has been since 09-05 10:03, the section printed `uncommitted work in ~/mc/connections-section/memoro: hop-measure.mjs, probe.mjs | 09-05 10:03 · 7 h | step exit 143, no-json (09-05 10:06)` — the four things the instruction asks for. Then by hand: a file written into the clean `~/mc/cold-restore-integrity/memoro` produced `… mc-verify-scratch.txt | 09-05 16:38 · 0 min | no run recorded` (that project has never run, and the reading says so rather than borrowing another's row), and removing the file took the line away, leaving `connections-section` alone. The seven briefs those runs wrote were deleted from `~/mc/brief/`, so `lastBriefTime` is back at 2026-09-04T16:10:01Z. `npm test`: 1 725 tests, 1 716 pass, 0 fail, 9 skipped.

For step 5's close-out: the brief's own doc is already written — `docs/technical/mc-brief.md` has the twelfth section in its source table and a paragraph on why it is not rows in *Held before merge*. What is left there is `mc-run.md` and `mc-status.md`. `canon/roles/brief.md` gained the paragraph the instruction asked for, with a test in `tests/mc/commands/brief.test.js` binding it the way the other three sections are bound. No banner at the top of the brief for these rows: *Held before merge*'s banner exists because that section is ninth in a long file and its rows demand a decision the same hour, and the mechanism against skimming past this one is the role file, which is what the instruction named.

steps.title: Measure the killed-session question and put it
steps.done_when: The PR carries the measurement of how often a session leaves work uncommitted, what it leaves, and one recommendation on whether the runner should commit it itself — with the cost of each option named.
instruction: This step writes no recovery mechanism. It answers whether one is wanted, with numbers, because the honest position today is that a killed session's worktree is not obviously the runner's to commit — the work may be half a refactor — and not obviously a person's either, and so it is nobody's.

Measure the estate rather than reasoning about it. `~/mc/runner/log/runs.tsv` has every run: find every row that ended `no-json`, exit 143, or exit 0 with `pr=-`, and for each check whether its workarea was left dirty and for how long it stayed that way before somebody acted. `mail-window-overlay-integrity` ended exit 143, 5 408 s, `no-json` at 2026-09-05T08:02:48Z and left its worktree **clean** — that session had committed — so the answer is not "every killed session", and the proportion is the number this step exists to produce.

Two instances of the pattern already exist in the estate and both are evidence: `09cfbfa655` on `no-text-in-code`, a WIP commit made by hand, and `ac32169675` on `connections-section` — *"WIP: org in the portrait tile — superseded by ruling 4, kept for the record"* — made by a session by itself. Read both and say what they cost and what they saved.

Name the options and the cost of each: leave it to a person and rely on step 3's brief line to find it; commit it to the branch as a WIP commit named for the run that left it, so the next step session inherits it; or refuse the project until a person acts, which is what happens today but loudly. The middle one has the hazard worth stating plainly — a WIP commit of half a refactor is work the next session must judge before it can proceed, and a session that cannot tell finished work from abandoned work will build on top of it.

One recommendation, not three options and a shrug. Put it in the PR body where Martin reads it. If he rules, carry the ruling into `docs/project/mc/rulings.md` in the same shape the file already uses — the question, the options, his answer quoted verbatim — because mc keeps no record of an answer anywhere else.
Nothing in this step changes behaviour, so there is nothing to verify beyond the measurement being reproducible: say in the PR which commands produced the numbers.
comments: The measurement, over `runs.tsv` and `runner.log` for 2026-08-25 → 2026-09-05 (574 runs, 451 of them `step` or `repair`): **17 step runs left the workarea dirty, 3.8 %**. Of the 114 step runs that opened no pull request, 73 were the 3–5 s quota-refusal cluster and are noise; of the 41 real ones, **14 left dirt (34 %)**. Of the 12 runs killed at budget (exit 143 / `no-json`), **6 left dirt (50 %)** — so the plan's premise is right, it is not every killed session, and `mail-window-overlay-integrity` at 2026-09-05T08:02:48Z is confirmed one of the six that had committed. Time from the run to somebody acting, in hours, over the 17: 0.1 0.7 3.9 4.3 6.6 7 8.4 9 11.3 13 18.2 19.7 57.5 59.5 93.5 110.4 122.1 — **median 11.3 h**, and 1 017 rounds skipped on a dirty worktree in the whole log. The rate is ~1.4 episodes a day. The method: a run left it dirty iff the *next* `runner.log` line for that project is a `dirty worktree` skip, which attributes the dirt to one run rather than to any run before it; the episode ends at the first non-dirty line for the project. Two episodes have no closing line because the project stopped being walked, and git supplied the end for both (`home-on-msr` 110.4 h to commit `474e6555`; `inbox-finish` still uncommitted at 67.8 h).

What the dirt is, from the eight episodes whose file list `runner.log` carries (the list was added 2026-09-04) plus the surviving worktrees: three shapes and not one. **Real work** — `no-text-in-code` 35 files, `email-verification-round` 34 files / 1 920 insertions, `inbox-finish` 6 files / 165 insertions including a test and two docs, `home-on-msr` 107 files / 26 141 insertions of which nearly all are regenerated `sdk/corpus/` JSON behind a 957-line capture script. **Pure scratch** — `mail-window-overlay-integrity` (`mwoi-probe.tmp.mjs, mwoi-slices.tmp.sh, mwoi-sum.tmp.mjs +1`) and `connections-section` (`hop-measure.mjs`, `probe.mjs`, 110 lines of untracked measuring script), between them 43 skipped rounds for files nobody wanted. **Bookkeeping** — `connections-section` on 2026-09-04 stood 11.3 h on one modified `PLAN.json`.

The recommendation, and it is the answer to the step's question: **leave the commit to a person; do not build the runner's own recovery.** The evidence is what the person adds. Six hand-made recovery commits exist in twelve days — `09cfbfa6`, `700a3edc`, `2f120ad3`, `a3982d19`, `ac321696`, `474e6555` — and four became merged pull requests within three hours of the commit (memoro #11396, #11414, #11294, memoro-cli #439), while two were deliberately archived and have never reached main: `ac321696` says *"superseded by ruling 4 … nothing here is meant to land"* and `474e6555` is a generated corpus that the repository's own rule says is produced by its script, not carried by hand. Every one of the six carries a verdict on the work in its message, and that verdict is exactly what a session killed at budget cannot write and the runner cannot infer — it has the exit code and nothing else. A blind WIP commit would have been right four times, noise twice, and would have put superseded work and 26 000 lines of regenerated corpus on the branch for the next step session to inherit silently. The cost of leaving it is named and real: the median 11.3 h standstill stays, and roughly one project is stopped this way at any given time.

What makes the recommendation defensible *now* rather than in general is that the two multi-day standstills — `connections-section` 122.1 h and `home-on-msr` 110.4 h — were invisibility and not unwillingness, and steps 1–3 of this project removed the invisibility three days after the last of them. Nobody has yet been slow to act on a dirty workarea that a surface named. So the trigger for revisiting is a number: if over a fortnight of the brief's *Ready, and the runner cannot start it* section the median time-to-clean does not fall to a few hours, the shape to build is the narrow one — commit only on exit 143, never on a clean exit, and onto `wip/<project>-<run-ts>` rather than the project branch, so the next step session has to reach for it.

One gap in the surfaces this project built, found by the measurement and worth knowing before step 5 writes the docs: `inbox-finish` has held 6 files and 165 insertions of apparently finished work since its session was killed at 2026-09-02T20:59:43Z, and **no surface names it**, because its `PLAN.json` does not parse (`what_the_code_taught_us: unknown key`, `steps[1].pr`). `waitingOnHands` filters to `RUN_REFUSALS`, so an unparseable plan is a *Plan status* row and its dirty workarea is nobody's line. That is correct as designed — the plan is the first thing wrong there — but it means the worst single loss in the measurement is the one the new section cannot show.

No ruling was asked for or given here; the session that has Martin's answer writes it into `docs/project/mc/rulings.md` in that file's shape, and this step deliberately did not pre-write the entry. Separately, the scratch half of the finding is a proposal rather than a paragraph of this plan: `~/mc/proposals/2026-09-05-scratch-files-stop-the-round.md` argues for a `$MC_SCRATCH` outside the worktree and one sentence in `canon/roles/_common.md`, on the ground that two of the eight episodes cost 43 rounds for throwaway files and the round's dirty check should not be softened to fix it.

instruction: Write the distinction down where the next reader meets it, because it is the thing this project exists to make legible and it is not obvious from either function's name: `planState` answers *is this plan ready to be worked on*, and it is a fact about a file on `main`; the new reading answers *would the runner start it now*, and it is a fact about this machine at this moment. Neither can answer the other's question, and that is why there are two.
Say which surfaces show the pair and which show only the plan, so a reader knows what a bare `ready` means wherever they meet one.
Add the row to `docs/project/project_log.md`.
